# PicoCalc Tetris

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A Tetris game for the **ClockworkPi PicoCalc**, by **Thomas Dzubin**, written
in C against the **Raspberry Pi Pico SDK** and the driver layer from
[`picocalc-text-starter`](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by **Blair Leduc** (LCD, audio and south-bridge keyboard drivers) — vendored
here under [`picocalc-text-starter-main/`](picocalc-text-starter-main/).

```
tetris.c                     the whole game
tetris_config.h              every #define, tunable and constant data table (piece shapes,
                             gravity speeds, music, sound effects)
CMakeLists.txt               builds the firmware, reusing picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/*
desktop/                     Desktop (SDL2) build, Windows and Linux: CMakeLists.txt + the small shim that
                             stands in for the PicoCalc drivers
pico_sdk_import.cmake        standard Pico SDK locator (copied from the starter)
picocalc-text-starter-main/  vendored driver layer (see License; do not edit)
LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md        MIT licence; version history
```

## Where this came from

This is an **original, from-scratch implementation** written after
reverse-engineering the real Game Boy Tetris ROM in Ghidra. No
code, data tables, graphics or music from that ROM are copied here — only
*concepts confirmed by decompiling it* were carried over into fresh code:

- **10x18 board** — the real Game Boy field size (most other versions,
  NES included, use 10x20).
- **Scoring**: 40 / 100 / 300 / 1200 points for a single / double / triple /
  tetris line clear, multiplied by `(level + 1)`. This exact table was found
  live in the ROM's decompiled code.
- **Piece randomizer**: pick a random next piece; if it would repeat the
  immediately-previous piece, re-roll up to two more times before giving up
  and allowing the repeat. The real ROM seeds this from the Game Boy's
  free-running `DIV` register — there's no such register here, so this
  project seeds its own PRNG from the Pico's free-running microsecond timer
  instead. The full method is described under "How pieces are chosen" below.
- **No wall kicks** — a rotation that doesn't fit is simply rejected
  ("classic" rotation, as opposed to modern SRS-with-kicks).

Deliberately **not** reproduced, since it would cross from "inspired by"
into "a copy of" the commercial game and wasn't needed for the mechanics:
exact frame-perfect gravity/DAS timing (approximated to feel right, not
measured), and monochrome Game Boy-accurate visuals (pieces get their own
colours here since the PicoCalc has a colour LCD).

## How pieces are chosen

Each new piece comes from `pick_next_piece()` in `tetris.c`:

1. A small random number generator (xorshift32, `rng_next()`) supplies the
   numbers. The Pico's free-running microsecond timer is mixed into it
   (`rng_stir()`) when the program starts and again at the start of every
   game, at the moment the player presses a key on the splash screen. That
   keypress time is unpredictable, whereas the timing at power-up alone is
   almost the same every time. The generator then keeps running from one game
   to the next.
2. A number from 0 to 6 is drawn (the random value modulo 7), one for each of
   the seven pieces: I, O, T, S, Z, J and L.
3. If the draw is the same piece as the one that was just dealt, it is thrown
   away and a new number is drawn, up to two more times (three draws in all).
   After the third draw, whatever came up is used, even if it is a repeat.
4. The piece chosen is the "next" piece shown in the preview. When the current
   piece locks, the preview piece becomes the falling piece and the following
   one is chosen against it. The very first piece of a game is a plain draw,
   because there is no previous piece to avoid.

What this means in play, checked by simulating two million picks with the same
algorithm:

| Measure                                              | Result                                   |
|------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Same piece twice in a row                            | 0.3% (exactly 1 in 343); plain random would give 14.3% |
| Long-run share of each piece                         | 14.3% each, all seven equal              |
| After any piece, chance of each of the other six     | 16.6% each (57 in 343)                   |
| A piece missing from the next 14 picks after it appears | about 9% (roughly 1 in 11)            |
| A piece missing from the next 20 picks after it appears | about 3% (roughly 1 in 32)            |
| Longest gap seen for one piece in two million picks  | 68 pieces                                |

There is no "bag" (dealing out all seven pieces in a shuffled set before
reshuffling). The generator remembers nothing except the previous piece, so
droughts and floods of a particular piece can happen. Only back-to-back repeats
are suppressed.

## Music

The background music is **"Korobeiniki"** ("The Peddlers"), the Russian folk
song that made Tetris famous — but the *tune itself* is an 1800s folk melody,
public domain in its own right, independent of Nintendo's specific game
arrangement of it. `tetris.c`'s `MELODY[]` is this project's own
transcription of that public-domain tune, played by a small non-blocking
sequencer. Press **M** any time in-game to mute it.

## Controls

| Key             | Action                              |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------|
| LEFT / RIGHT    | move the falling piece (auto-repeats) |
| DOWN            | soft drop (fall faster while held)   |
| SPACE           | rotate clockwise                     |
| UP              | rotate counter-clockwise (opposite of SPACE) |
| ENTER or P      | pause / resume                       |
| M               | mute / unmute the music              |
| Q               | pause and ask "QUIT GAME?": **Y** exits the program (back to the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu; on Windows/Linux it closes the window), any other key resumes. On the splash screen Q asks the same question; any other key then starts a game |
| ESC             | quit to the splash screen            |
| ~ (SHIFT + `)   | reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode |

## Building

VS Code Pico extension (Compile / Run), or from a terminal with `PICO_SDK_PATH`
set:

```
cmake -B build -G Ninja
ninja -C build
```

Output: `build/picocalc-tetris-<chip>.uf2` (`<chip>` is `RP2350` or `RP2040`, matching the board), which the build also copies to the
top-level folder as `picocalc-tetris-RP2350.uf2` or `picocalc-tetris-RP2040.uf2`
(depending on `-DPICO_BOARD=pico2` / `pico`), so both chips' builds can sit side
by side. Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2` drive — hold BOOTSEL on power-up, or
press `~` (SHIFT + backtick) in the app.

### Windows

The same game runs on Windows through a small SDL2 layer in
[`desktop/`](desktop/) that stands in for the PicoCalc's LCD, keyboard and
audio drivers. From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2 installed:

```
cmake -S desktop -B build-windows -G Ninja
ninja -C build-windows
```

Output: `picocalc-tetris-Windows.exe` in the top-level folder. SDL2 is linked
statically, so it is a single file with no `SDL2.dll`. The keys are the same as
the table above (`~` simply closes the program).

### Linux

The same source builds on Linux with the SDL2 development package installed
(for example `sudo apt install libsdl2-dev`). Unlike the Windows build, SDL2 is
**not** linked in statically: the program links `libSDL2` dynamically, and the
build copies that library next to the executable as `libSDL2-2.0.so.0`, where
the executable finds it through an `$ORIGIN` run-path. Keep the two files
together.

    cmake -S desktop -B build-linux
    cmake --build build-linux

Output: `picocalc-tetris-Linux` and `libSDL2-2.0.so.0` in the top-level folder.
